This is something that has always bugged me about digital media. I really hate the idea that I'm only paying a licensing fee to consume the media on approved platforms. It makes me wonder if MP3 players (iPod) would have become as huge as they did as quickly or as soon as they did if no one ripped their music libraries.

If everyone sat around going "Gee, it's really wrong if I copy the music from the CD I purchased to the computer I purchased. That would be unfair to the musicians" then we'd all still be using boomboxes to listen to our music. I'll pay for content, I'll do so happily. I pay for a few web development tutorial websites because I like their content and I want to support them. It really sealed the deal when I found out that I could download the lessons and watch later without any DRM nonsense. I keep hoping musicians and other artists will one day get their chance at killing off the giant distribution corporations so we can finally have direct access between creators and consumers.

I keep hoping musicians and other artists will one day get their chance at killing off the giant distribution corporations so we can finally have direct access between creators and consumers.

These companies will never die, but I ask you, do they need to? They create jobs, which, disgusting as their work might be, are valuable. And now, here in the internet age, content creators have ways to work around these licensing companies in a way they never have been able to. Yes, Sony as a company is scum, and a fucking cancer to creative development (for instance, thanks to a false positive contentID match, Sony Music now owns the sound I make when I cough, not me), but they are no longer our only option. If you look on youtube, beatport, bandcamp, soundcloud, and dozens of other sites, big and small, you see individuals pushing their own music, or in some cases, larger channels working to promote individual artists by collecting similar musicians' work into one place, which is, remember, exactly how Sony formed in the first place, but here, their presence can only be good. Where do we draw the line? Or do we just ignore the bad, try to prevent them from doing damage to the good, and let everyone promote their music as they choose. That's my preferred option, though I do have plenty of reason to hate certain companies *cough* Sony *cough cough* (oops). Doesn't keep me from calling them out on their bullshit, though.

You are right that people do have the right to associate with whatever company they choose. If a band or musician wants to work with Sony, that's their choice. I don't want them to die as in we all blackball them, I would prefer to have the waste and greed gone. However, I do believe the overreach (Sony's rootkit fiasco) is spurred by the size of the company. It would be nice if more people, myself included, knew and used alternative sources for purchasing music (including physical discs). I want a market that compels companies to avoid the underhanded tactics because one mistake could sink the company, a market where they can't afford to be shady.
